Practical memory improvement from O(mn) to O((m+n)r̂) by combining variance-reduced momentum with randomized SVD
Batch size 1 efficiency throughout training, unlike Muon++ requiring batch size O(ε⁻¹)

Well-structured comparison table (Table 1) positioning the work relative to recent Muon variants

Assumption 5 is restrictive and poorly justified: requires tail singular values bounded by gradient norm but provides no empirical evidence this holds during neural network training or analysis of robustness to violations

Significant theory-practice gap: RSVD approximation error not fully integrated into convergence proofs; theoretical convergence to stationarity not validated in short experiments that don't reach convergence

strengths: Comprehensive convergence analysis under both standard Lipschitz smoothness and generalized (L₀, L₁)-smoothness conditions, providing theoretical foundations for the approach

Broad empirical evaluation across diverse architectures (Mamba, Qwen, ViT)

strengths: Addresses an important practical problem: memory efficiency in optimizer design for large models
Provides comprehensive theoretical analysis with convergence proofs across multiple settings (Lipschitz smooth, generalized smooth, Newton-Schulz variants)

weaknesses: Significant theory-practice gap: Theoretical O(ε⁻³) sample complexity not validated empirically; memory savings predicted ~16× but achieved only ~9% on Mamba-130M

Incomplete baseline comparisons: Muon++ (the key variance-reduced variant) lacks side-by-side evaluation under identical conditions; missing wall-clock time comparisons for language models
Soundness issues: Low-rank SVD approximation introduces unbiased gradient estimates in STORM-style updates; restrictive learning rate requirement η ≤ O(1/r) may negate practical benefits
Limited novelty: Combines STORM (Cutkosky & Orabona 2019) and randomized SVD (Halko et al. 2011); main contribution is application to Muon rather than new techniques

Questionable experimental trends: Non-monotonic performance across ranks (Table 2) suggests instability; no confidence intervals or multiple random seeds; statistical significance not established
Presentation clarity: Distinction between Option #1 (full M_t, no memory savings) and Option #2 confusing; theorems mix both without clear purpose for Option #1

Well-motivated problem addressing genuine limitations of existing Muon variants regarding memory-complexity trade-offs
Practical algorithmic design with two options (full-rank and low-rank) providing flexibility, simpler than Muon++ without gradient clipping
Solid experimental validation across diverse architectures (Mamba, Qwen2.5, ViT) demonstrating competitive performance and 10-15% memory savings

Limited novelty: paper combines two existing techniques (STORM variance reduction + randomized SVD); while sensible, core ideas are not new
